title: Push notifications with Firebase Cloud Messaging
tagline: Which message type shows a popup, in which app state, and which handler runs.
intro: FCM delivers the message; what the user sees depends on the message type and on whether the app is open, in the background or quit. Most confusion comes from mixing those up.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: A message's path from Firebase to the screen.

blocks.caption: Who handles a remote notification at each step.

items.label: Server sends
items.detail: Your backend or the Firebase console sends a message addressed to one device token
explain: The token identifies one install of the app on one device. messaging().getToken() returns it, and the backend stores it against the user.
The payload is a notification block, a data block, or both. That choice decides everything after this step.

items.label: FCM delivers
items.detail: FCM routes it to the device, through APNs on iOS, which is why iOS needs push certificates
explain: On iOS, Apple's APNs is the only way in. The bundle id needs the Push Notifications capability, and Firebase needs the APNs key or certificate.
On Android, Google Play services receives it and wakes the app, as long as the user has not force-stopped it.

items.label: OS shows it
items.detail: A notification payload in background or quit is drawn by the OS, without your code
explain: This is the only case where a popup appears with no JavaScript involved: the OS reads title and body and draws them.
On Android the popup only drops down if the notification's channel has high importance; otherwise it goes straight to the tray.

items.label: Your handler runs
items.detail: onMessage in foreground, setBackgroundMessageHandler otherwise, and nothing is drawn for you
explain: In the foreground FCM never shows a popup, even for a notification payload. onMessage fires and the app decides.
To show one anyway, call a local notification library such as react-native-push-notification from inside onMessage.

sections.title: iOS setup
sections.summary: Apple has to allow pushes before Firebase can send them.

items: Create the Firebase project and download GoogleService-Info.plist
Create the bundle id in Apple Developer → Identifiers with Push Notifications enabled
Create a provisioning profile that includes a real device, then download it in Xcode

body: The iOS simulator cannot receive remote pushes from APNs on older Xcode versions, so test on a real device.

items: Send test messages from testfcm.com without writing a backend
Android 8+ files every notification under a channel. Without one it lands in the tray silently.
Create the channel before any notification can arrive — at module load, above the App component.
Importance.HIGH is what lets it drop down as a heads-up popup.

blocks.caption: Notification: the OS can draw it on its own
Notification + data: drawn by the OS, with extra fields for your code
Data only: never drawn, always handed to your code
